docs.title: robot_lab-discovery
docs.text:
Zero-configuration mDNS/DNS-SD robot discovery for RobotLab on local networks.

Robots advertise themselves via multicast DNS (mDNS, RFC 6762) and find each other without any central registry, hardcoded URL, or configuration file. Each robot announces a name, an HTTP path, and a free-form set of capability tags; other robots (or any process on the LAN) can browse for all of them, look one up by name, or filter by capability.

require "robot_lab/discovery"

# A robot announces itself:
adv = RobotLab::Discovery::Advertiser.new(
  name: "headline", port: 9292, path: "/headline",
  capabilities: ["writing", "research"]
)
adv.start

# Anyone on the LAN can find it:
result = RobotLab::Discovery.find("headline", timeout: 5)
result.url   # => "http://my-server.local:9292/headline"

This gem augments robot_lab-a2a but has no dependency on it. The gemspec declares two runtime dependencies — core robot_lab (~> 0.6) and the pure-Ruby zeroconf gem. require "robot_lab/discovery" loads core robot_lab only to register itself as an extension; the discovery code itself calls nothing but zeroconf. Discovery finds you a URL; you decide what protocol to speak to it (A2A, plain HTTP, anything else).

docs.title: At a Glance
docs.text: Protocol Multicast DNS / DNS-SD (RFC 6762 / RFC 6763), pure Ruby — no Bonjour/Avahi/system daemon Service type _robot-lab._tcp.local. Advertise RobotLab::Discovery::Advertiser.new(name:, port:, path:, capabilities:).start Discover RobotLab::Discovery.browse / .find / .find_by_capability / .list_capabilities Result RobotLab::Discovery::Result — name, hostname, port, path, capabilities, #url Scope LAN-only — a single multicast subnet, not routable across the internet Runtime dependencies robot_lab ~> 0.6, zeroconf ~> 1.3 Core integration require "robot_lab/discovery" requires core robot_lab and self-registers via RobotLab.register_extension(:discovery, ...)

docs.text:

docs.title: API Reference
docs.text: Every public class, module, and method in robot_lab-discovery. See How It Works for the concepts and wire-level detail behind each one.

docs.title: RobotLab::Discovery (module)
docs.text: Top-level convenience methods — thin delegators to Browser, plus two standalone utility methods.

docs.title: browse(timeout: 3) → Array<Result>
docs.text:
All robots currently visible on the LAN, deduplicated by name. Delegates to Browser.browse.

RobotLab::Discovery.browse(timeout: 3).each { |r| puts r.url }

docs.title: find(name, timeout: 5) → Result, nil
docs.text: Polls (see How It Works) until a robot named name appears or timeout elapses. Returns nil if it never appears. Delegates to Browser.find.

docs.title: find_by_capability(cap, timeout: 3) → Array<Result>
docs.text: Robots advertising capability cap, found by browsing that capability's DNS-SD subtype directly (a real network-level filter, not client-side). Delegates to Browser.find_by_capability.

docs.title: list_capabilities(timeout: 3) → Array<String>
docs.text: Every capability string currently advertised by any robot on the LAN, exactly as advertised (not dns_label-normalized), deduplicated and sorted (Ruby's default case-sensitive String order). Delegates to Browser.list_capabilities.

docs.title: dns_label(capability) → String
docs.text:
Normalizes a free-form capability string into a valid DNS label: downcased, non-alphanumeric runs collapsed to a single hyphen, no leading/trailing hyphen.

RobotLab::Discovery.dns_label("Web Search")        # => "web-search"
RobotLab::Discovery.dns_label("NLP/Analysis")      # => "nlp-analysis"
RobotLab::Discovery.dns_label("Web Search / NLP")  # => "web-search-nlp"

docs.title: validate_capabilities!(capabilities) → Array<String>
docs.text:
Coerces capabilities (an array, a single value, or nil) to an array of strings and returns it. Raises ArgumentError if any capability contains a comma (it would be split in two when the TXT record is decoded) or contains no ASCII letter or digit (its dns_label would be empty). Called by Advertiser.new.

RobotLab::Discovery.validate_capabilities!(%i[research writing])  # => ["research", "writing"]
RobotLab::Discovery.validate_capabilities!(["a,b"])               # raises ArgumentError

docs.title: Error
docs.text: RobotLab::Discovery::Error < StandardError — raised only by TxtRecord.validate! and TxtRecord.validate_capabilities_content! (see below) when a TXT record exceeds its size limits.

docs.title: Constants
docs.text:
Constant Value Meaning SERVICE_TYPE "_robot-lab._tcp.local." the one DNS-SD service type every robot registers under, regardless of name or capabilities VERSION "0.6.1" the gem version; also written into every TXT record as v= 
RobotLab::Discovery::SERVICE_TYPE  # => "_robot-lab._tcp.local."

docs.title: RobotLab::Discovery::Advertiser
docs.text: Announces one robot over mDNS.

docs.title: new(name:, port:, path:, hostname: Socket.gethostname, capabilities: [])
docs.text:
Parameter Type Default Description name String (required) mDNS instance name. Must not contain dots — not checked here, but #start raises ArgumentError (from zeroconf) if it does. port Integer (required) port the robot's server listens on path String (required) HTTP path to the robot; stored in the TXT record, not validated by this gem hostname String Socket.gethostname the host name to advertise as the SRV target; zeroconf strips any trailing .local and advertises "<hostname>.local." capabilities Array<String>, String [] free-form taxonomy terms; coerced to an array of strings and checked by Discovery.validate_capabilities! — raises ArgumentError for one that contains a comma or has no ASCII letter or digit

Only validates capabilities and assigns instance variables — no network activity happens until #start is called.

docs.title: Constants
docs.text: Constant Value Meaning START_TIMEOUT 5 default seconds #start waits for the service thread to announce or fail STOP_TIMEOUT 5 default seconds #stop waits for the service thread to exit before killing it

docs.title: start(timeout: START_TIMEOUT) → self
docs.text: Builds a ZeroConf::Service for SERVICE_TYPE, encoding path:/capabilities: into the TXT record via TxtRecord.encode (raises RobotLab::Discovery::Error here if the record is too large — see How It Works) and registering one DNS-SD subtype per capability. Spawns the actual service on a background Thread, then waits until it has sent its announcement, has finished, or timeout seconds have passed (normally a few milliseconds) and returns self. An error raised on that thread while the service is starting is re-raised here (and kept in #error); zeroconf's ArgumentError for a dotted name: is raised here too.

docs.title: stop(timeout: STOP_TIMEOUT) → self
docs.text: Stops the ZeroConf::Service (sends an mDNS goodbye packet, TTL=0) and joins the background thread for at most timeout seconds; a thread that still has not exited is killed and joined again for up to timeout seconds, so stop never blocks indefinitely — including when called immediately after start. By the time stop returns, advertising has ended. Safe to call when not started.

docs.title: started? → Boolean
docs.text: true while the background thread is alive; false before start, after stop, or once the thread has died from an error (see #error).

docs.title: Attributes
docs.text:
name, port, path, hostname, capabilities — all readers, reflecting the values passed to new (capabilities after coercion to an array of strings).

error — the StandardError that ended the background thread, or nil. Reset to nil by each start.

docs.title: RobotLab::Discovery::Browser (module)
docs.text: Stateless class methods that do the actual mDNS browsing and response parsing. RobotLab::Discovery.browse/find/find_by_capability/list_capabilities are thin delegators to these.

docs.title: browse(timeout: 3) → Array<Result>
docs.text: ZeroConf.browse(SERVICE_TYPE, timeout:), parsed into Results, deduplicated by name. Always returns an array — [] when zeroconf hands back nil.

docs.title: find(name, timeout: 5) → Result, nil
docs.text: Polls browse in ≤1-second increments until name matches or timeout elapses; nil on timeout. See How It Works for why this is a real loop, not a single call.

docs.title: find_by_capability(capability, timeout: 3) → Array<Result>
docs.text: Browses "_#{dns_label(capability)}._sub.#{SERVICE_TYPE}" instead of the base service type.

docs.title: list_capabilities(timeout: 3) → Array<String>
docs.text: browse(timeout:).flat_map(&:capabilities).uniq.sort — a plain case-sensitive String sort of the capability strings as advertised.

docs.title: parse_response(response) (private — not part of the public API)
docs.text: Extracts SRV (port, hostname, instance name) and TXT (path, capabilities) data from a raw mDNS response and builds a Result. Returns nil for a malformed/partial response (missing SRV or missing path) rather than raising — this is why callers use filter_map, not map. Documented here only because CLAUDE.md calls it out explicitly: do not call this directly; it's an implementation detail of browse/find_by_capability.

docs.title: RobotLab::Discovery::Result
docs.text:
Result = Data.define(:name, :hostname, :port, :path, :capabilities)

An immutable value object — every field below is a plain reader; there are no writers. Defined directly under RobotLab::Discovery with a url method added in the Data.define block.

Field Type Description name String mDNS instance name hostname String fully-qualified .local hostname (trailing DNS root dot already stripped) port Integer port the robot's server listens on path String HTTP path to the robot capabilities Array<String> capability taxonomy terms this robot advertises ([] if none)

docs.title: url → String
docs.text: "http://#{hostname}:#{port}#{path}". Always plain HTTP — this gem has no notion of a scheme beyond that; build the URL yourself if a robot serves over HTTPS.

docs.title: RobotLab::Discovery::TxtRecord (module)
docs.text: Encodes/decodes the DNS TXT record payload. Normally used internally by Advertiser/Browser; documented publicly because the wire format and size limits are useful to understand when debugging a discovery issue or building a compatible advertiser in another language.

docs.title: Constants
docs.text: Constant Value Meaning PATH_KEY "p" wire key for the HTTP path VERSION_KEY "v" wire key for the gem's version at encode time CAPABILITIES_KEY "c" wire key for the comma-joined capability list MAX_STRING_BYTES 255 RFC 1035 §3.3.14 per-string limit — not configurable MAX_TOTAL_BYTES 1300 wire-size budget kept under the UDP/Ethernet MTU to avoid fragmentation MAX_CAPABILITIES_CONTENT 253 bytes available for the capabilities string's content (255 - "c".bytesize - "=".bytesize)

docs.title: encode(path:, capabilities: []) → Array<String>
docs.text: Builds ["p=#{path}", "v=#{VERSION}"], appending "c=#{capabilities.join(',')}" only when capabilities is non-empty, then validates the result via validate! (raising RobotLab::Discovery::Error on a size violation) before returning it. The comma-joined capabilities are checked first by validate_capabilities_content!.

docs.title: validate_capabilities_content!(content) → String
docs.text: Raises RobotLab::Discovery::Error if content (the comma-joined capability list, without its c= key) is larger than MAX_CAPABILITIES_CONTENT bytes; returns content unchanged otherwise. Called internally by encode.

docs.title: decode(strings) → Hash
docs.text: Parses an array of "key=value" strings (splitting on the first = only, so a value itself containing = round-trips correctly) into {path:, rl_version:, capabilities:}. Unknown keys are silently ignored. :capabilities is only present in the returned hash when a c= entry existed — absent, not [], when there wasn't one.

docs.title: validate!(strings) → Array<String>
docs.text: Raises RobotLab::Discovery::Error if any single string exceeds MAX_STRING_BYTES, or if the total wire size (sum of (1 + bytesize) across all strings, accounting for each string's length-prefix byte) exceeds MAX_TOTAL_BYTES. Returns strings unchanged when valid. Called internally by encode; exposed publicly for callers who build TXT string arrays some other way.

docs.title: Extension registration
docs.text: require "robot_lab/discovery" requires core robot_lab and calls RobotLab.register_extension(:discovery, RobotLab::Discovery), so RobotLab.extension_loaded?(:discovery) returns true regardless of require order.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Ruby 4.0.9+ (per the gemspec's required_ruby_version)
  • A multicast-capable network interface — standard on any LAN. zeroconf is pure Ruby and implements mDNS itself over standard UDP multicast sockets; it does not wrap Bonjour, Avahi, or any system mDNS daemon, so there is nothing else to install.
  • Core robot_lab (~> 0.6) is a declared gem dependency, so Bundler installs it alongside this gem. require "robot_lab/discovery" requires it for you and self-registers as an extension via RobotLab.register_extension(:discovery, ...), whatever order you require things in.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
bundle add robot_lab-discovery

Or add to your Gemfile directly:

gem "robot_lab-discovery"

Then:

bundle install

docs.title: Advertising a Robot
docs.text:
require "robot_lab/discovery"

adv = RobotLab::Discovery::Advertiser.new(
  name:         "headline",              # mDNS instance name — no dots allowed
  port:         9292,
  path:         "/headline",             # stored in the TXT record
  hostname:     Socket.gethostname,      # default; advertised as "<hostname>.local"
  capabilities: ["writing", "research"]  # free-form taxonomy terms
)

adv.start   # begins advertising in a background thread; raises if the service fails to start
# ... your server runs ...
adv.stop    # sends an mDNS goodbye packet (TTL=0); removes it from peers' caches

start spawns the actual ZeroConf::Service on a background Thread, waits (normally a few milliseconds, at most timeout: seconds — default 5) for it to send its announcement, and returns self — the service loop itself never blocks your server's main thread. If the service fails while starting (a socket error, say), start re-raises that error instead of leaving a dead thread behind. stop asks the service to exit and joins that thread with a bounded wait, killing it if it hasn't exited after timeout: seconds (default 5), so stop cannot hang and it's safe to assume the service is torn down once stop returns — even when called immediately after start.

Capability strings are free-form — see How It Works — Capability Taxonomy for the (light) conventions worth following. Each one is normalized into a valid DNS label ("Web Search" → "web-search") and registered as a DNS-SD subtype, so peers can browse for it directly without scanning every robot on the network. Two things are rejected by Advertiser.new with an ArgumentError: a capability containing a comma (the comma is the TXT-record separator) and one with no ASCII letter or digit (it would normalize to an empty label).

docs.title: Discovering Robots
docs.text:
require "robot_lab/discovery"

# All robots on the LAN
results = RobotLab::Discovery.browse(timeout: 3)
results.each { |r| puts "#{r.name}: #{r.url}  caps=#{r.capabilities.join(', ')}" }

# Find one robot by name (polls until found or timeout)
result = RobotLab::Discovery.find("headline", timeout: 5)
result.url            # => "http://my-server.local:9292/headline"
result.capabilities   # => ["writing", "research"]

# Find all robots offering a specific capability
researchers = RobotLab::Discovery.find_by_capability("research", timeout: 3)

# List every capability type currently advertised on the LAN
RobotLab::Discovery.list_capabilities(timeout: 3)
# => ["analysis", "coding", "research", "writing"]

All four are blocking calls — each one waits (up to timeout seconds) for mDNS responses to arrive over the network before returning. None of them should be called from a request thread that needs to stay responsive; see Key Constraints below.

docs.title: Connecting After Discovery
docs.text:
Result#url is a plain URL string — wire it to whatever client you use:

result = RobotLab::Discovery.find("headline")

# With robot_lab-a2a:
client = A2A.client(url: result.url)
client.send_task(message: A2A::Models::Message.user("Summarise today's news"))

# With Net::HTTP directly:
Net::HTTP.get(URI(result.url))

docs.title: Running the Bundled Example
docs.text:
examples/01_basic_usage.rb walks through the complete lifecycle end to end — registering three robots with different capabilities, browsing all of them, finding one by name, finding by capability, listing the capability inventory, then unregistering:

bundle exec ruby examples/01_basic_usage.rb

Both the advertisers and the browser run in the same process in that example purely for demo convenience — in production, each robot's own server process runs its own Advertiser, and any separate process (a dashboard, an orchestrator, another robot) does the browsing.

docs.title: Development
docs.text:
bundle install
bundle exec rake test     # run the test suite (Minitest::Reporters::SpecReporter output)
bin/console                # IRB with the gem loaded

Tests mock the zeroconf interactions (ZeroConf.stub(:browse, ...)) — no actual mDNS traffic is sent while running the suite.

docs.title: Key Constraints
docs.text:
• mDNS is LAN-only. It works within a single multicast subnet — it does not cross routers, VPN tunnels, or cloud network boundaries. There is no equivalent of this gem for discovery across separate networks.
  • Other mDNS clients can hold stale records after a crash. If a robot's process crashes without calling Advertiser#stop, no goodbye packet is sent, so caching mDNS stacks elsewhere on the LAN (Bonjour, Avahi, and tools built on them) keep its records until their TTL (60 seconds) expires. This gem's own browse/find keep no cache — each call sends a fresh query and returns only the robots that answer it — so a crashed robot simply stops appearing in their results.
  • find polls in a blocking loop. It repeatedly calls browse internally until the named robot appears or timeout elapses — see How It Works — find(name, timeout:). Don't call it from a thread (a web request handler, an event loop) that needs to stay responsive.
  • Capability content is capped. All capabilities for one robot are joined into a single comma-separated TXT string capped at 253 bytes of content (TxtRecord::MAX_CAPABILITIES_CONTENT). Many short capability names comfortably fit; very long strings or a huge number of them will raise RobotLab::Discovery::Error at Advertiser#start (via TxtRecord.encode/validate_capabilities_content!) — see How It Works for the exact limits.
  • Instance names may not contain dots. name: becomes the mDNS instance name; DNS-SD instance names are dot-separated internally (name._robot-lab._tcp.local.), so zeroconf rejects a name: containing a literal . — Advertiser#start raises ArgumentError ("instance_name must not contain dots"). Advertiser.new itself does not validate the name.

docs.title: The mDNS/DNS-SD Model
docs.text:
This gem is a thin, purpose-built layer over two RFCs:

  • mDNS (RFC 6762) — DNS queries and responses sent over UDP multicast on the local subnet (224.0.0.251:5353), instead of to a unicast DNS server. Any host on the same LAN segment hears every query and response.
  • DNS-SD (RFC 6763) — a convention for naming services within DNS: a service type (_robot-lab._tcp.local.), an instance name, and a TXT record carrying arbitrary key/value metadata alongside the usual SRV record (which carries the target host and port).

RobotLab::Discovery::SERVICE_TYPE is "_robot-lab._tcp.local." — every robot advertised by this gem, regardless of name or capabilities, registers under that one DNS-SD service type. A browser listening for that type hears every robot on the LAN; capability-specific browsing (below) narrows that with DNS-SD subtypes instead of a second protocol.

The zeroconf gem (the only dependency the discovery code itself calls into — core robot_lab ~> 0.6 is required solely so the gem can register itself as an extension) implements both RFCs itself in pure Ruby over a raw UDP socket — there is no Bonjour/Avahi/system daemon involved and nothing to install beyond the gem itself.

docs.title: Advertising: Advertiser
docs.text:
adv = RobotLab::Discovery::Advertiser.new(name:, port:, path:, hostname: Socket.gethostname, capabilities: [])
adv.start

start builds a ZeroConf::Service for SERVICE_TYPE with:

  • instance_name: — the name: you gave (becomes the DNS-SD instance name)
  • text: — the TXT record, built by TxtRecord.encode(path:, capabilities:) (see below)

  • subtypes: — one "_#{dns_label(capability)}" string per capability

  • started_callback: — a lambda the service calls once it has sent its announcement

...then spawns @service.start on a background Thread and waits — up to timeout: seconds (Advertiser::START_TIMEOUT, 5, by default; in practice a few milliseconds) — for that callback, or for the thread to finish, before returning self. The service loop itself runs on the background thread and never blocks the caller. If the thread raised while starting, start cleans up and re-raises that error in the caller; an error raised later, after start has returned, ends the thread, is kept in Advertiser#error, and makes started? return false. stop calls @service.stop (which makes the service send the mDNS goodbye packet — a response with TTL=0 telling every listening peer to drop this record from its cache right away) and then joins the thread for at most timeout: seconds (Advertiser::STOP_TIMEOUT, 5, by default). ZeroConf::Service#stop does nothing until the service has marked itself started, so if the thread is still alive after that wait, stop kills it (the service's own ensure still sends the goodbye and closes its sockets) — stop therefore never hangs, and by the time it returns the advertising thread has exited. started? reports @thread&.alive? || false.

docs.title: Subtypes: How Capability Browsing Actually Works
docs.text:
DNS-SD subtypes are a real part of the spec, not something this gem invents: a service can register as belonging to _robot-lab._tcp.local. and to any number of _<subtype>._sub._robot-lab._tcp.local. names simultaneously. Advertiser#start registers one subtype per capability — a robot advertising ["writing", "research"] shows up under:

_robot-lab._tcp.local.                          (always)
_writing._sub._robot-lab._tcp.local.
_research._sub._robot-lab._tcp.local.

Discovery.find_by_capability("research") browses _research._sub._robot-lab._tcp.local. directly — the mDNS query itself only reaches robots registered under that subtype, so this is a real network-level filter, not a client-side filter over every robot's TXT record. Discovery.browse/list_capabilities, by contrast, browse the base _robot-lab._tcp.local. type and see every robot regardless of capability.

docs.title: The TXT Record Wire Format
docs.text:
TxtRecord encodes three possible fields into the DNS TXT record, using single-character keys to conserve UDP packet space:

Wire key Meaning Long-form equivalent avoided p path path= (saves 3 bytes) v rl_version (the gem's VERSION at encode time) rl_version= (saves 9 bytes) c capabilities, comma-joined capabilities= (saves 11 bytes)

encode(path:, capabilities: []) always includes p= and v=; c= is omitted entirely when capabilities is empty (not encoded as c=). decode(strings) reverses this, splitting each "key=value" string on the first = only (so a path containing = round-trips correctly — "p=/foo=bar" decodes to path: "/foo=bar"), and silently ignores any key it doesn't recognize (forward-compatible with future fields). capabilities is only present in the decoded hash when a c= entry existed at all — decode(["p=/x"]) returns a hash with no :capabilities key, not capabilities: []; Browser.parse_response is what supplies the [] default via txt.fetch(:capabilities, []) when building a Result.

docs.title: Size Limits, and Why They Exist
docs.text:
Two limits are enforced from inside encode — the general ones by TxtRecord.validate!, the capability budget by TxtRecord.validate_capabilities_content!:

  1. Per-string: 255 bytes (MAX_STRING_BYTES). This isn't a design choice — it's RFC 1035 §3.3.14: every string inside a TXT record is length-prefixed with a single byte, so no individual string can exceed 255 bytes no matter what. Since capabilities all share one c=... string, MAX_CAPABILITIES_CONTENT (255 - "c".bytesize - "=".bytesize = 253 bytes) is the real budget for however many comma-separated capability names you pack in. encode checks that budget itself, via TxtRecord.validate_capabilities_content!, before the generic per-string check — so an over-long capability list fails with a message that names the capability limit.
  2. Total wire size: 1300 bytes (MAX_TOTAL_BYTES). This one is a design choice, derived from the physical network: mDNS runs over UDP, and a standard Ethernet MTU (1500 bytes) minus IP/UDP/DNS header overhead leaves roughly 1472 bytes for the whole DNS payload. After the SRV and A/AAAA records that accompany every service announcement also claim space in that same packet, keeping the TXT record itself under 1300 bytes (wire size = 1 length-prefix byte + content bytes, summed across every string) leaves enough headroom that the whole announcement stays inside a single unfragmented UDP packet. encode alone can never actually reach this second limit — three strings, each capped at 255 bytes, tops out well under 1300 — so this check exists to protect callers who build TXT string arrays some other way and hand them to validate! directly, not a realistic failure mode of encode itself.

All of these violations raise RobotLab::Discovery::Error with a message naming the exact byte count, at Advertiser#start time (since that's when TxtRecord.encode runs) — not at Advertiser.new time, since the constructor only checks each capability's form (see Capability Taxonomy); it does not encode anything.

docs.title: Discovering: Browser
docs.text: Browser is a module of class methods — there's no instance to hold, since browsing is stateless per call.

docs.title: browse(timeout:)
docs.text: Calls ZeroConf.browse(SERVICE_TYPE, timeout:), which blocks for up to timeout seconds collecting raw mDNS responses (on the rare occasion zeroconf returns nil instead of a list, that is treated as no responses), then maps each one through the private parse_response and drops any that come back nil (filter_map), then deduplicates by name (uniq(&:name) — a robot that responds more than once during the browse window, which is normal for mDNS, only appears once in the result).

docs.title: find(name, timeout:)
docs.text:
deadline = Time.now + timeout
loop do
  remaining = deadline - Time.now
  return nil if remaining <= 0
  result = browse(timeout: [remaining, 1].min).find { |r| r.name == name }
  return result if result
end

This is a polling loop, not a single browse call with a longer timeout: it repeatedly calls browse in increments of at most 1 second ([remaining, 1].min), checking after each one whether the named robot showed up, until either it's found or the overall timeout has elapsed. The 1-second cap keeps each individual browse responsive rather than committing the whole remaining budget to one blocking call; the practical effect is that find returns at the end of the increment in which the target robot answers (each browse call always blocks for its full increment), rather than always waiting out the full timeout.

docs.title: find_by_capability(capability, timeout:)
docs.text: Normalizes capability via RobotLab::Discovery.dns_label, browses "_#{label}._sub.#{SERVICE_TYPE}" — the DNS-SD subtype, not the base service type — and otherwise behaves exactly like browse (parse, filter, dedupe by name).

docs.title: list_capabilities(timeout:)
docs.text: browse(timeout:).flat_map(&:capabilities).uniq.sort — every capability string across every currently-visible robot, exactly as advertised (not dns_label-normalized), deduplicated and sorted with Ruby's default case-sensitive String ordering ("Web Search" sorts before "data analysis").

docs.title: parse_response(response) (private)
docs.text: Given a raw Resolv::DNS::Message-like response, walks response.answer + response.additional looking for an SRV record (supplies port, hostname — with the trailing . FQDN dot stripped — and the instance name, taken from the first label of the resource name) and a TXT record (decoded via TxtRecord.decode). If either the SRV data or a path from the TXT data is missing, it returns nil rather than raising — a malformed or partial mDNS response is simply skipped, not an error condition, which is why browse uses filter_map rather than map.

docs.title: RobotLab::Discovery::Result
docs.text:
Result = Data.define(:name, :hostname, :port, :path, :capabilities) do
  def url = "http://#{hostname}:#{port}#{path}"
end

An immutable value object (Ruby's Data.define, not a mutable Struct or hash) — every Result a browse/find/find_by_capability call returns is a fresh, frozen snapshot with no field writers (note that the capabilities array it holds is not itself frozen). url always assumes plain http:// — this gem has no notion of TLS and doesn't encode a scheme in the TXT record; if a robot actually serves over HTTPS, build the URL yourself from the other fields rather than using #url directly.

docs.title: dns_label
docs.text:
def self.dns_label(capability)
  capability.to_s.downcase.gsub(/[^a-z0-9]+/, "-").gsub(/\A-+|-+\z/, "")
end

Downcases, collapses every run of non-alphanumeric characters to a single hyphen, then strips any leading/trailing hyphen left over. "Web Search" → "web-search"; "NLP/Analysis" → "nlp-analysis"; "Web Search / NLP" → "web-search-nlp" (the / and its surrounding spaces form one non-alphanumeric run, so together they collapse into a single hyphen). This is what turns a free-form capability string into something legal to use as a DNS label component in a subtype name — DNS labels can't contain arbitrary punctuation, spaces, or mixed case in a way every resolver treats consistently.

docs.title: Capability Taxonomy
docs.text: Capabilities are free-form strings — there is no enforced registry or fixed vocabulary anywhere in this gem. Only two things are rejected, by RobotLab::Discovery.validate_capabilities! when Advertiser.new runs, each with an ArgumentError: a capability containing a comma (capabilities are comma-joined in the TXT record, so it would decode as two) and a capability with no ASCII letter or digit (dns_label would reduce it to an empty subtype label). The convention (not an enforced rule) is short, lowercase, hyphen-separated terms describing what a robot does, not how it works internally — e.g. research, analysis, writing, coding, vision, memory, tool-use, orchestration, web-search, summarisation, classification. A robot can advertise any number of them; each becomes its own DNS-SD subtype (see above), so clients browsing by capability only ever hear from robots that actually advertise it — no client-side filtering of the full robot list is needed.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text: RobotLab::Discovery::Error (a plain StandardError subclass) is raised only by TxtRecord — by validate!, when either the per-string or total wire-size limit is exceeded, and by validate_capabilities_content!, when the comma-joined capabilities exceed their 253-byte budget (see above). There's no other error class in the gem: an unusable capability raises a plain ArgumentError from Advertiser.new, and Advertiser/Browser let any underlying zeroconf/Resolv/socket error propagate as-is rather than wrapping it (for example, zeroconf raises ArgumentError from Advertiser#start when name: contains a dot). An error raised on the advertising thread while the service is starting is re-raised by Advertiser#start; one raised later is available from Advertiser#error.

docs.title: Key Constraints (and Why)
docs.text:
These follow directly from the mechanics above, not from arbitrary gem-level restrictions:

  • LAN-only, by protocol, not by choice. mDNS multicast packets don't cross routers (that's what makes them "local" — RFC 6762 explicitly scopes them to the local link). There is no configuration in this gem that extends reach beyond a single multicast subnet; a VPN, a different VLAN, or a cloud network boundary will not see these announcements at all.
  • Stale records in other mDNS caches after an ungraceful crash. Advertiser#stop sends an explicit goodbye packet that tells peers to evict the record immediately. A process that dies without calling stop (a kill -9, a crash) never sends that packet — its record simply sits in the cache of any caching mDNS stack on the LAN (Bonjour, Avahi) until that record's TTL (60 seconds, as announced by zeroconf) expires on its own. This gem's own browse/find keep no cache: every call sends a fresh query and returns only the robots that answer within timeout, so a crashed robot simply stops appearing — but a robot that answered a moment ago can still be gone by the time you connect, so a caller that needs liveness guarantees beyond "answered the last query" needs a mechanism this gem doesn't provide (e.g. an application-level heartbeat over whatever transport the discovered URL leads to).
  • find blocks the calling thread. It's a real polling loop (see above), not instant — even a successful lookup returns only when its current polling increment (up to 1 second) finishes, not the instant the robot answers, and an unsuccessful one blocks for the entire timeout. Never call it from a thread that has to stay responsive (a web request handler, an event loop's main thread) without moving it to a background thread or job yourself.
  • Capability content is capped by the RFC 1035 per-string limit, not an arbitrary choice this gem made — see Size Limits above for the exact numbers and where they come from.
